(C) The lead agency’s records.
(3) Upon completing the search required by paragraph
(2), the lead agency shall provide consulting tribes all
information obtained pursuant to paragraphs (1) and
(2), as well as an invitation to meet and confer pursuant
to paragraph (4).
(4) After receiving the information provided by the lead
agency pursuant to paragraph (3) and upon the request
of a consulting tribe, the consulting tribe, lead agency,
and applicant shall meet and confer regarding the
proposed essential project and any known or recorded
tribal cultural resources, and a consulting tribe may
share any information, including information in tribal
government registers. During the meet and confer, the
three parties shall identify and evaluate treatment and
protection methods, measures, and conditions to
address impacts on tribal cultural resources, including
avoidance and preservation in place. Unless otherwise
agreed upon by all parties, any agreements among all
the parties from the meet and confer shall be finalized
during the tribal consultation process set forth in
subdivision (d). The results of the meet and confer shall
be documented and maintained by the lead agency in
agreement with the consulting tribe.
(5) (A) If a consulting tribe does not respond to the
initial screening invitation provided by the lead agency
pursuant to paragraph (3) within 30 days, the initial
screening process pursuant to this subdivision shall be
deemed to have concluded and the parties shall move
into the tribal consultation process set forth in
subdivision (d). A consulting tribe’s decision not to meet
and confer under the initial screening process in this
subdivision shall in no way affect the consulting tribe’s
ability or right to participate in the tribal consultation
process set forth in subdivision (d).
(B) The initial screening process provided in this
subdivision shall end when the tribal consultation
process set forth in subdivision (d) begins.
(C) Where the tribal consultation process set forth in
subdivision (d) does not apply, the initial screening
process under this subdivision shall terminate upon the
date of the parties’ agreement from the meet and
confer pursuant to paragraph (4) or 30 days from the
date an application for an essential project is
determined complete by the lead agency or deemed
complete by operation of law, whichever occurs first.
(d) Tribal consultation. Tribal consultation for an
essential project shall be conducted pursuant to
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 45 CONTINUED
Sections 21074, 21080.3.1, 21080.3.2, 21082.3,
21084.2, and 21084.3, except as modified as follows:
(1) The purpose of tribal consultation is to identify
tribal cultural resources and evaluate treatment and
protection measures for those tribal cultural resources,
including the implementation of treatment and
protection measures.
(2) Tribal consultation is not meaningful if the
consulting tribe is not provided with reasonably
requested technical information, including, but not
limited to, project information and constraints, data,
maps, and information concerning project activities as
they relate to treatment and protection of tribal cultural
resources. During tribal consultation pursuant to this
subdivision, the lead agency shall engage in iterative
discussions with the consulting tribe regarding the
development of mitigation measures related to tribal
cultural resources, including preliminary concepts or
approaches before publication of any draft
environmental document. This includes notifying the
consulting tribe of any existing technical studies or
reports in the lead agency’s possession that relate to
tribal cultural resources on or in the vicinity of the
essential project site, to the extent permitted by
applicable confidentiality laws, and providing the
consulting tribe with access to those studies or reports.
To the extent any draft environmental review document
is provided to the applicant for review in advance of the
public comment period for that environmental review
document, the draft shall also be made available to the
consulting tribe at the time it is provided to the
applicant. Nothing in this section shall be construed to
require the lead agency to prepare or circulate draft
environmental review documents for purposes of tribal
consultation.
(3) Where the lead agency, a consulting tribe, and the
applicant agree in writing to measures to avoid or
mitigate a significant effect on a tribal cultural resource,
those measures and any written agreement shall
become enforceable conditions of project approval,
subject to the confidentiality requirements under
paragraph (6) of subdivision (b).
(e) Treatment and protection of tribal cultural
resources. When feasible, damaging effects to any tribal
cultural resources shall be avoided. Consistent with
subdivision (b) of Section 21014, nothing in this
subdivision alters the lead agency’s obligation under
CEQA to avoid or mitigate significant impacts to tribal
cultural resources when feasible. Mitigation and
treatment measures adopted in consultation with the
consulting tribe pursuant to this subdivision to avoid or
minimize significant impacts to tribal cultural resources
shall be consistent with the following:
(1) Avoidance and preservation in place shall be
considered when requested by the consulting tribe. A
tribal cultural resource may be avoided or preserved in
place through project design, buffering, or other
protective measures to avoid the tribal cultural
resources and protect the cultural and natural context,
or planning greenspace, parks, or other open space to
incorporate the tribal cultural resources with culturally
appropriate protection and management criteria
referenced in the project’s environmental documents.
(2) If an essential project has the potential to cause a
substantial adverse change in the significance of a
tribal cultural resource, and avoidance and preservation
in place are not feasible, the lead agency shall
demonstrate and document the basis for that
determination with substantial evidence, and the
consulting tribe may identify culturally appropriate
mitigation measures that the lead agency shall consider
and incorporate, to the extent feasible, in developing
mitigation and treatment measures in a manner
consistent with paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of
Section 21084.3.
(3) When an essential project proposes construction-
related ground disturbance activities and when
requested by the consulting tribe, the lead agency shall
include inadvertent discovery measures to reduce
significant impacts to tribal cultural resources. Those
measures may include procedures for temporary halts
of grading, identification and assessment protocols,
timing provisions, and additional treatment methods or
protective measures.
(f) Essential project approval. A lead agency may only
approve an essential project pursuant to this section
when all of the following apply:
(1) Tribal consultation has concluded in good faith.
(2) Where there is agreement among all parties
pursuant to either paragraph (4) of subdivision (c) or
subdivision (d), any agreed upon mitigation and
avoidance measures are included as enforceable
project conditions.
(3) If avoidance and preservation in place is not
feasible, the lead agency has demonstrated and
documented the basis for that determination with
substantial evidence and incorporated other measures
to minimize impacts consistent with CEQA.
21017. Determining Completeness of Essential
Project Applications
(a) (1) When a public agency receives an initial
application for an essential project, the public agency
shall review the application, make a written finding
whether the application is complete, and notify the
applicant in writing of the determination.
(2) The written determination of completeness for an
initial application shall be made within 30 days of the
public agency’s receipt of the initial application. If the
public agency fails to provide a determination of
completeness within 30 days, then the initial application
shall be deemed complete for the purposes of this
division.
(3) An application shall not be determined to be
incomplete on the basis of (A) informational or
analytical studies or documents that were not required
by the public agency in a written, publicly available
submittal requirement checklist or similar document in
existence at the time the initial application was
45
Text of Proposed Laws | 161
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 45 CONTINUED
submitted or (B) statutes, regulations, rules, standards,
or ordinances that are not existing laws.
(b) If the public agency’s determination of
completeness finds that the initial application for an
essential project is incomplete, at the time that finding
is made the public agency shall also provide the
applicant with an exhaustive written corrections list
containing thorough descriptions of the items and
specific information, or lack thereof, that led to the
finding of incompleteness.
(c) (1) (A) The applicant shall, within 90 days of a
notification that its initial application is incomplete,
submit additional information or a revised application
that addresses the matters identified on the written
corrections list.
(B) If the applicant cannot comply with the 90-day
deadline in subparagraph (A) to submit either additional
information or a revised application, the applicant shall
notify the public agency in writing why it is unable to do
so and include an estimate of when it will be able
to do so.
(2) Upon any submission of supplemental information
or a revised application, the public agency shall
determine if the supplemented submittal is complete
based only on the written corrections list provided by
the agency pursuant to subdivision (b). The public
agency shall provide a determination of completeness
based upon the supplemented submittal within 30 days
of receipt thereof. If the public agency finds that the
supplemented submittal is still incomplete, at the time
that finding is made the public agency shall provide the
applicant with an updated exhaustive written
corrections list. The updated written corrections list
may only contain items included on the written
corrections list provided in response to the applicant’s
initial application.
(3) If a supplemented submittal is again deemed
incomplete, the applicant may submit additional rounds
of supplemental information or revised applications
pursuant to the procedures and timelines set forth in
this subdivision.
(4) If the public agency fails to provide a determination
of completeness within 30 days of receiving either
supplemental information or a revised application
pursuant to paragraph (2) or (3), the application shall
be deemed complete for purposes of this division.
(5) A public agency shall not request or require an
applicant to provide any new information unless that
information was included on the exhaustive written
corrections list for the immediately prior version of the
45
application.
(d) (1) A determination of completeness finding that
an initial application, supplemented application, or
revised application is incomplete shall be appealable by
the applicant to the public agency’s planning
commission, planning director, or other official with
final authority over application completeness. If the
public agency does not have a planning commission,
planning director, or other official with final authority
162 | Text of Proposed Laws
over application completeness, then the appeal shall be
heard by the highest-ranking elected or appointed
decisionmaking body or official of the agency. There
shall be a final written determination on the appeal not
later than 60 days after receipt of the applicant’s
written appeal.
(2) If the final written determination on the appeal is
not made within the 60-day period described in
paragraph (1), the application shall be deemed
complete for the purposes of this division.
(e) The applicant may bring a civil action challenging
an adverse determination under subdivision (d). Any
action shall be commenced within 90 days of an
adverse final written determination issued pursuant to
subdivision (d).
Article 4. Review of Completed Applications
for Essential Projects
21018. Local Agency Timeline for Completing
Environmental Review of Essential Projects
(a) A local agency that is acting as a lead agency (local
lead agency) for an application or approval of an
essential project shall decide whether the project is
subject to subdivision (b), (c), or (d) within 30 days of
the essential project application being determined or
deemed to be complete pursuant to Section 21017, or
deemed complete pursuant to any other law, whichever
occurs first.
(b) Essential projects that require an environmental
impact report. For essential projects that require an
environmental impact report, the local lead agency shall
make a final determination whether to certify an
environmental impact report no later than 365 days
after the essential project application being determined
or deemed to be complete pursuant to Section 21017,
or deemed complete pursuant to any other law,
whichever occurs first.
(c) Essential projects that require a negative
declaration or mitigated negative declaration. For
essential projects that require a negative declaration or
mitigated negative declaration, the local lead agency
shall make a final determination whether to adopt a
negative declaration or mitigated negative declaration
no later than 180 days after the essential project
application being determined or deemed to be complete
pursuant to Section 21017, or deemed complete
pursuant to any other law, whichever occurs first.
(d) For all other environmental review documentation
prepared pursuant to this division for an application or
approval of an essential project, the local lead agency
shall, within 90 days after the essential project
application being determined or deemed to be complete
pursuant to Section 21017 or deemed complete
pursuant to any other law, whichever occurs first, make
a final determination that the essential project is
exempt from this division or that the essential project’s
impacts were previously evaluated under a prior
environmental review document pursuant to, without
limitation, Section 21083.3 or 21094.5, or an
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 45 CONTINUED
addendum pursuant to Section 15162 or 15164 of
Title 14 of the California Code of Regulations.
(e) The deadlines set forth in subdivisions (b), (c), and
(d) shall be extended upon written request from the
applicant.
21019. Timeline for Completing Environmental
Review of Essential Projects by Public Agencies That
Are Not Local Agencies
(a) A public agency other than a local agency that is
acting as a lead agency (nonlocal lead agency) for an
essential project shall decide whether the project is
subject to subdivision (b), (c), or (d) within 30 days of
the essential project application being determined or
deemed to be complete pursuant to Section 21017, or
deemed complete pursuant to any other law, whichever
occurs first.
(b) Essential projects that require an environmental
impact report. For essential projects that require an
environmental impact report, the nonlocal lead agency
shall make a final determination whether to certify an
environmental impact report no later than 365 days
after the essential project application being determined
or deemed to be complete pursuant to Section 21017,
or deemed complete pursuant to any other law,
whichever occurs first.
(c) Essential projects that require a negative
declaration or mitigated negative declaration. For
essential projects that require a negative declaration or
mitigated negative declaration, the nonlocal lead
agency shall make a final determination whether to
adopt a negative declaration or mitigated negative
declaration no later than 180 days after the essential
project application being determined or deemed to be
complete pursuant to Section 21017, or deemed
complete pursuant to any other law, whichever occurs
first.
(d) For all other environmental review documentation
prepared pursuant to this division for an application or
approval of an essential project, the nonlocal lead
agency shall, within 90 days after the essential project
application being determined or deemed to be complete
pursuant to Section 21017 or deemed complete
pursuant to any other law, whichever occurs first, make
a final determination that the essential project is
exempt from this division or that the essential project’s
impacts were previously evaluated under a prior
environmental review document pursuant to, without
limitation, Section 21083.3 or 21094.5, or an
addendum pursuant to Section 15162 or 15164 of
Title 14 of the California Code of Regulations.
(e) The deadlines set forth in subdivisions (b), (c), and
(d) shall be extended upon written request from the
applicant.
21020. Noncompliance with Timelines for Completing
Environmental Review of Essential Projects
(a) When a local lead agency or a nonlocal lead agency
fails to comply with a deadline set forth in subdivisions
(b) to (d), inclusive, of Section 21018, or subdivisions
(b) to (d), inclusive, of Section 21019, the applicant
may make a written request for the agency to hold a
meeting or hearing on the essential project as provided
in this section.
(b) Within 60 days of receipt of a written request
pursuant to subdivision (a), the local lead agency or
nonlocal lead agency shall do all of the following:
(1) Complete all environmental review documentation
for the essential project or assemble available
environmental review documentation, including any
applicant-prepared environmental review document as
is allowed pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section
21082.1 or any other law.
(2) Hold a meeting or hearing on the essential project
application as follows:
(A) If the agency has a multimember decisionmaking
body subject to the Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act
(Article 9 (commencing with Section 11120) of Chapter
1 of Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government
Code), the Ralph M. Brown Act (Chapter 9 (commencing
with Section 54950) of Part 1 of Division 2 of Title 5 of
the Government Code), or similar open meeting law, the
agency shall place the essential project on its agenda
for a regular or special meeting of the agency’s highest-
ranking decisionmaking body.
(B) If the agency does not have a multimember
decisionmaking body subject to the Bagley-Keene Open
Meeting Act, the Ralph M. Brown Act, or a similar open
meeting law, then the highest-ranking official of the
agency, or their designee, shall hold a hearing with the
applicant on the essential project.
(3) Notwithstanding any other provision of this division
or any other law, at the meeting or hearing described in
paragraph (2), the agency shall do both of the following:
(A) Make a final written determination on the available
environmental review documentation that has been
completed as of the date of the meeting or hearing.
(B) Make a final written determination to approve or
disapprove the essential project.
(c) (1) If the local lead agency or nonlocal lead agency

Endorsement: CEQA is a mess. Prop 45 is even messier
Proposition 45 would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects and potentially make it easier to build environmentally ruinous projects.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 17, 2026
What’s the most polarizing four-letter word in California politics?
CEQA.
That wasn’t always the case. When then-Gov. Ronald Reagan signed the California Environmental Quality Act into law in 1970, the need could not have been more obvious. Californians were fed up with planners bulldozing low-income neighborhoods and communities of color for miles of polluting freeways. They were horrified by the ecological damage and habitat destruction caused by suburban sprawl. They were tired of top-down infrastructure projects that left communities feeling disempowered and voiceless.
CEQA laid out a basic protective framework: Before approving a project, government officials needed to evaluate potential negative environmental impacts and identify ways to mitigate or avoid them while providing ample opportunity for public review and input.

But it didn’t take long for the law to be easily manipulated for ends that had little or nothing to do with the environment.
NIMBYs used the process to delay new infill housing — driving up costs and reducing the likelihood projects get built. Unions leveraged CEQA to extort favorable labor terms on projects (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/california-housing-union-labor-17802611.php). Courts showed a predisposition for allowing just about anything to become grounds for a CEQA challenge — which is how we ended up with a 2022 lawsuit against a UC Berkeley housing project (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-UC-Berkeley-students-are-now-16931016.php) that effectively branded students as a form of pollution.
This editorial board has repeatedly decried CEQA abuses and has urged politicians to take decisive action (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/uc-berkeley-peoples-park-housing-ceqa-newsom-17816129.php).
In recent years, they have, to a degree.

State lawmakers passed, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed, bills to, among other things, permit more units on many single-family-home lots (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/California-cities-rush-to-limit-new-law-16647764.php), streamline the development of dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/sb79-now-law-fight-affordable-housing-goes-21094908.php), exempt almost all infill housing from CEQA (https://sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) and speed up permitting timelines for large clean-energy projects (https://modelclimatelaws.org/resources/californias-sb-205-2022/).
But it’s still far too easy to bury certain essential projects in delay, litigation and costly uncertainty.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf), placed on the November ballot via signatures gathered by the California Chamber of Commerce, would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop45-110326.pdf) its authors deem “essential”: housing, water (other than the Delta tunnel (https://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/will-california-ever-build-the-delta-tunnel-22237021.php)), clean energy (excepting nuclear power), healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation (other than high-speed rail).
How would the measure aid these kinds of projects?
First, it establishes a litany of strict deadlines — some of which are technically already in CEQA but rarely enforced. Government agencies, for example, would have 30 days to determine whether a project application is complete, 365 days to conduct an environmental review and decide whether to certify it and 90 days to decide on permits. If agencies fail to meet these deadlines, applicants could trigger a public hearing within 60 days, at which time a final decision must be made. Applicants can sue if agencies don’t follow these procedures.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 45 also significantly reduces paperwork. Government agencies could no longer repeatedly ask developers for more information to determine whether an application is complete — they would have one chance to produce an “exhaustive written corrections list.” Agencies would also be prohibited from changing the criteria or scope of their assessments mid-review. Agencies would no longer have to come up with multiple alternatives to environmentally impactful projects; instead, the applicant would propose just one alternative. The measure also restricts the public comments that can be included in the administrative record.
Finally, Prop 45 permits courts to halt only portions of a project determined to have “a specific, adverse impact upon public safety.” If courts sign off on an environmental review, no further lawsuits would be allowed. Lawsuits, including appeals, would need to be resolved within 270 days, with a possible 90-day extension.
In aggregate, these changes are far bigger in scope than any previous CEQA reform.
Some of the stipulations are eminently reasonable.
Enforcing deadlines is a no-brainer, as is eliminating excess paperwork and reducing frivolous litigation. Project applicants are not entitled to approvals, but they are entitled to decisions being made in a timely manner.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Furthermore, some of the projects Prop 45 seeks to streamline — like public transit, bike lanes and infill housing — are objectively good for the environment. They shouldn’t be subject to extreme CEQA scrutiny.
Others, however, are beyond questionable.
Prop 45 applies its streamlining process to freeway expansions and greenfield housing development in wildfire zones. And why does it specifically exempt the one transportation project that arguably needs the most help: California’s voter-approved high-speed rail, which is years behind schedule and billions over budget thanks in part to costly CEQA challenges? (https://grist.org/transportation/billions-spent-miles-to-go-the-story-of-californias-failure-to-build-high-speed-rail/)
Poll testing, said Emma Manoukian Chung, a strategist for the Yes on Prop 45 campaign. There was “voter appetite” for freeways and sprawl, but not high-speed rail.
But throwing a grab bag of poll-tested projects together and suggesting they should be evaluated on substantially similar terms is neither reasonable nor good policy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Huge infrastructure projects — such as freeways and dams — have fundamentally different environmental impacts than infill housing. And infill housing has different environmental consequences than single-family homes in car-centric, high-wildfire-risk zones.
It makes no sense to apply the same scrutiny and deadlines to each.
It’s also unclear whether Prop 45 applies to data centers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/data-centers-artificial-intelligence-dakotas-22362642.php). Opponents insist the “broadband internet access” category leaves open the possibility, while proponents insist that it doesn’t.
Ultimately, that question will likely have to be answered through litigation — ironically, the very thing Prop 45 is trying to curb.
It’s also ironic that Prop 45, despite aiming to reduce uncertainty, actually creates much more of it.
“This is deep, deep, deep in the weeds of environmental law,” Chris Elmendorf, a UC Davis law professor and one of California’s preeminent CEQA experts, told us. “It’s a super complicated body of law that they’re trying to change, trying to make it easier to build stuff.
“Some of the changes are good and some may be bad, and who knows what kind of second-order effects they will have?”
That’s why the state Legislature is best suited to handle complicated, nuanced policy, tweaking laws as needed — unlike the all-or-nothing blunt instrument of the ballot box.
“An initiative should be considered a last resort … when the Legislature is doing nothing,” Prop 45 opponent Darrell Steinberg, a former Sacramento mayor and state Senate leader, told us. But, he said, “just the opposite” is occurring.
We agree.
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, particularly when it comes to housing, transportation and green energy projects. Some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45.

Prop 45 is poll-tested political Swiss cheese, not a thoughtful effort to produce better outcomes. Vote no.

Prop. 45 promises more housing. Why are some YIMBYs against it?
The ballot measure would speed up environmental reviews for housing and much more. Usual allies are split over whether that’s worth the trade.
Laura Foote, right, is executive director of YIMBY Action, whose members are split on Prop. 45.

For years, the YIMBY playbook in California has been simple: If it makes it easier to build housing, back it.
But one statewide measure doesn’t fit so neatly.
Proposition 45 could usher in one of the biggest changes in decades to California’s landmark environmental protection law. The California Environmental Quality Act was designed to protect the environment by requiring government agencies to examine the impacts of development.
ADVERTISEMENT
But critics have long argued that it has become a powerful weapon for opponents of new housing, allowing projects to be delayed for years or derailed entirely.
A “yes” vote on Prop. 45 (https://sfstandard.com/2026-election-voter-guide/proposition/45/) would reshape that process by setting firm timelines on environmental reviews and lawsuits on housing and other “essential” projects, a category that covers everything from apartment buildings to water systems, freeways, and broadband infrastructure.
For California’s pro-housing movement, which has spent years fighting to loosen CEQA’s grip on development, the measure might seem like an obvious victory. Instead, it has exposed a surprising divide over just how far those reforms should go.

Opponents have seized on the broadband category in political ads, linking the measure to the unpopularity of data centers, which have galvanized communities (https://sfstandard.com/2026/08/28/data-center-backlash-silicon-valley/) across the country and state.
But the YIMBY debate over Prop. 45 runs deeper. While the coalition broadly agrees that CEQA has been weaponized for decades to delay housing construction, some worry that the measure’s sweeping changes would also benefit polluters and encourage sprawl, undermining the movement’s broader commitment to combating climate change.
That’s why YIMBY Action and California YIMBY have taken a “no recommendation” stance — reflecting divisions among their members.
“Let the record show that I am not a dictator,” quipped Laura Foote, executive director of YIMBY Action, who is personally voting for Prop 45.

Max Dubler, policy manager for CA YIMBY, wrote this (opens in new tab) (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/) in his “No Recommendation” paper:
Whether this is a good idea depends on how you weigh the tradeoffs: is permitting new wind and solar energy infrastructure faster worth making it easier to build freeways? Should we make it easier to build transmission lines to carry that clean energy to consumers, even if it means potentially impacting wildlife habitat? Narrowing the focus to housing, the central question here is how you feel about sprawl.
Other pro-housing advocates such as Jordan Grimes are outright against Prop. 45. In an op-ed (opens in new tab) (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/09/12/opinion-vote-no-prop-45-would-take-away-our-best-defense-against-corporate-polluters/) in The Mercury News, the legislative director at Greenbelt Alliance argued that last year’s AB 130 (https://sfstandard.com/2025/07/07/san-francisco-ceqa-reform-newsom-wiener-abundence/) already exempts (https://sfstandard.com/2025/07/07/san-francisco-ceqa-reform-newsom-wiener-abundence/)nearly all infill apartment projects from CEQA.

“Prop. 45 isn’t about affordability or the housing crisis,” Grimes wrote. “It’s about handing shortcuts to polluting industries that they’ve wanted for years, disguised as relief for Californians struggling with the cost of living.”
Grimes also argues that CEQA is something the state Legislature should tackle at a policy level rather than voters making blanket changes with unintended consequences.
But the Housing Action Coalition, whose members helped craft the measure, supports Prop. 45. While acknowledging AB 130 as a victory for YIMBYs, the group argues that the ballot measure would cement broader CEQA reforms rather than leave lawmakers to pursue them piecemeal, bill by bill.
State laws have increasingly tilted in developers’ favor as the housing crisis has worsened. | Source: Getty Images “In an ideal world where everyone can compromise and agree to build within cities, this wouldn’t be necessary,” said Corey Smith, executive director of HAC. “But that didn’t happen. We need to make moves that help us win.”
AB 130, which focused on urban infill projects, is limited to sites less than 20 acres. Supporters of Prop. 45 say that it doesn’t cover larger-scale projects such as the Hillsdale Mall, the former Vallco Mall, or Stonestown Galleria redevelopments (https://sfstandard.com/2024/09/11/southwest-san-francisco-tale-of-two-cities/) . Furthermore, opponents can still challenge CEQA exemptions that the law grants in court.
The No on Prop. 45 campaign (opens in new tab) (https://www.noprop45ca.com/coalition#p45-coalition-toggle) is supported by a coalition of labor, health, and environmental organizations and 19 members of the state legislature. One of its top funders is Wendy Schmidt, the wife of former Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

Recently, the campaign has intensified its focus on data centers — arguing that compressed environmental reviews would make them easier to develop.
In a statement this week, the campaign took issue with the measure’s definition of “essential projects,” which includes broadband internet infrastructure. Opponents argue that the language could extend to data centers.
“The Legislature just spent a year writing data center safeguards, and Prop. 45 could significantly undermine that effort,” said Matthew McKerley, an attorney at Shute, Mihaly & Weinberger, which specializes in government, land use, and environmental law.

But the Yes on 45 campaign disputes that interpretation. It pointed to an opinion last week (opens in new tab) (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/legopinion_DataCenter.pdf) published by the state’s nonpartisan Office of Legislative Counsel, which reviewed the definition of term in relation to the net neutrality and said that data centers are not included in the definition of “broadband internet access service” under the government code.
Applied to Prop. 45, the Yes campaign says the measure incorporates the Federal Communications Commission’s definition.

Kurt Oneto, an attorney and the measure’s official proponent, writing for the National Law Review (opens in new tab) (https://natlawreview.com/article/prop-45-does-not-cover-data-centers-heres-why) this month, said supporting the internet doesn’t make data centers broadband projects, any more than supplying lumber makes a sawmill a housing project.
Prop. 45 does explicitly carve certain projects out of its definition of “essential,” including the Delta tunnel, nuclear power, jails and high-speed rail. It does not alter any local zoning.
If approved, the measure, backed by the California Chamber of Commerce, would impose strict deadlines throughout the CEQA process Environmental impact reports would have to be finished within 365 business days; public comment periods would be capped at 45 days, and lawsuits would have to be filed within 30 days and fully resolved, including appeals, within 270 days.
Projects have been stalled for years or, in some cases, abandoned because the CEQA process in the past allowed some actors to turn the exercise into an endless debate.
Related

Full environmental reviews would be required only for projects that exceed measurable thresholds established under existing environmental laws. The measure would also restrict both the arguments and evidence that could be presented in court challenges, potentially giving an advantage to developers.
Foote argues that CEQA is a poor tool for protecting the environment.
“You’re making every developer do a book report that you can sue them on,” she said.

Political action committees funded by technology companies, the state’s major utilities and other corporate interests have spent several million dollars more to pass a ballot measure that would greenlight major development projects with minimal environmental or public review than public interest and labor groups have spent opposing it.
Developers and other corporate interests aim to streamline the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA (https://www.califaep.org/docs/CEQA_Handbook_2023_final.pdf), which requires public agencies to identify, disclose and mitigate a development project’s negative impacts on a wide range of environmental resources, including wildlife, air and water quality and tribal cultural resources.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf) shifts who determines the scope of environmental review from public agencies and communities to project developers by rewriting the state’s foundational environmental law to fast-track major projects.
Supporters of Prop 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, have spent at least $36 million to pass the measure, the most recent state records show. Opponents, led by a coalition of more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations, have spent about $30 million to defeat what they say will give polluters a free pass.

“Prop 45 will modernize the approval process for essential projects by establishing clear, enforceable timelines for agency decisions and court challenges,” the chamber said in promotional materials, “while keeping environmental protections intact and preserving worker protections, tribal protections and local control.”
Critics say Prop 45 will gut the state’s primary vehicle for allowing people to learn about plans for polluting developments in their neighborhoods and propose alternatives.
“It undermines basically every stage of that process,” said Woody Little, the spokesperson for No on Prop 45.
Little and his allies say the 41-page ballot measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) was written by corporations who have paid to get their special interests on the ballot to create loopholes that favor polluting industries like recently regulated (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/21/governor-newsom-signs-most-comprehensive-data-center-laws-in-the-nation-providing-communities-more-control-on-water-electricity-and-land-use/) data centers while limiting the input of communities and local tribes.
Critics of CEQA, signed in 1970 by then-Gov. Ronald Reagan, blame the law for hobbling home construction and driving housing and cost of living increases in California, which are among the highest in the nation.
Prop 45 will lower housing and utility costs by reducing “endless” bureaucratic delays and protect taxpayers by reducing waste and cost overruns, Yes on Prop 45 materials argue.
Yet there is no requirement in the measure to reduce housing costs or utility bills. And the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) estimates that Prop 45 could leave state and local governments paying $100 million or more a year, partly to cover fast-tracked projects’ environmental impacts.
“The housing issue is a smokescreen for all these other polluting projects,” said Little.
California passed laws last year that significantly streamlined CEQA by exempting (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB130) urban and mixed-use housing construction from its provisions as well as certain infrastructure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB131) and clean energy (https://www.energy.ca.gov/programs-and-topics/topics/power-plants/opt-certification-program) projects.
“ I would hope that 100 percent of Californians would see this radical reshaping of California’s environmental law for the dangerous thing that it is. A wolf in sheep’s clothing.”
— Woody Little, No on Prop 45
None of the grassroots groups that promote “yes in my backyard,” or YIMBY (https://yimbyaction.org/), policies to build more housing and public transit in urban and suburban areas support Prop 45, Little said. Most are neutral, he said, while others oppose it.
Expanding housing beyond already developed areas means building new freeways, water connections and other expensive infrastructure that taxpayers ultimately pay for, Little said. And these projects often encroach on the wildland-urban interface, raising wildfire risk just as climate change is making fires more destructive.
At a time when California is already seeing the catastrophic costs of climate-fueled fires, Little said, the state should be requiring more environmental review around developments to assess and mitigate risk, not less.
What’s “Essential”?
Prop 45 covers nine types of “essential” projects, among them housing, water systems, clean energy (including carbon capture and storage), transportation, wildfire risk reduction and broadband internet access. All related and “ancillary” infrastructure is also covered.
Whether “ancillary” includes data centers, which typically require broadband infrastructure (https://tiaonline.org/how-broadband-workforce-development-and-standards-drive-data-center-growth/), has been a major point of contention.
Prop 45’s proponents have insisted the measure does not cover data centers, but legal experts disagree, pointing to $2 million in donations from just three data center builders and language buried in the measure’s 41 pages. Eligible projects include “broadband internet access projects,” defined as “mass-market retail service … that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all Internet endpoints,” a recent analysis (https://www.dailyjournal.com/articles/394431-prop-45-will-speed-data-center-construction) found.

That definition includes facilities that house the physical infrastructure used to transmit consumer data to and from the internet—which describes many data centers.
Yet data centers are conspicuously absent from the list of excluded controversial projects, which includes high-speed rail, the Delta Conveyance Project (https://www.deltaconveyanceproject.com/about-the-delta-conveyance-project), nuclear power and oil and gas facilities.
Inside Climate News asked the Yes on Prop 45 campaign why it sought to further limit environmental review after California had already significantly streamlined CEQA and why the measure does not explicitly exclude data centers. The campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
California Resources Corp., the state’s largest (https://www.crc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/california-resources-corporation-completes-acquisition-crimson) oil and gas producer, has donated $500,000 directly to Prop 45 campaigns and another $500,000 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1021742&session=2025&view=received) to a business committee sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce. Oil and gas facilities are explicitly excluded from Prop 45, but CRC has a data center under environmental review at its Elk Hills oil field.
CRC did not respond to questions about whether it supports Prop 45 in order to fast-track its data center application.
Protecting Community Voices
“Proposition 45 would weaken CEQA protections for the very projects that still warrant careful scrutiny—development that could put people in harm’s way, fragment wildlife habitat, threaten water resources or damage irreplaceable cultural and sacred sites,” environmental and conservation leaders argued in a recent op-ed (https://lookout.co/california-has-already-streamlined-ceqa-proposition-45-goes-too-far/story).
One of the op-ed authors, Chris Wilmers, tracks mountain lions as lead researcher for the Santa Cruz Puma Project. In his study area, retaliatory killings for preying on domestic animals and vehicle strikes are the biggest threat (https://lookout.co/mountain-lions-ucsc-researcher-chris-wilmers-on-how-new-highway-17-animal-crossing-protects-santa-cruz-mountain-lions/story) to mountain lions as new housing and roads continue to encroach on the wide-ranging carnivores’ critical habitat.
An adult male mountain lion travels through a tunnel under Highway 101, heading south toward California’s Santa Monica Mountains in 2018. Credit: National Parks Service
CEQA requires developers to weigh alternatives to mitigate harm if new evidence emerges that a project would degrade critical wildlife corridors or endangered species’ habitat. But such facts would never come to light under Prop 45, which lets developers write their own rules, Wilmers and others say.
And the ballot measure strips away the rights of tribes that aren’t recognized by the federal government to safeguard their sacred lands.
That leaves large swaths of California, including the Central Coast, the San Francisco Bay Area and much of the Los Angeles area, without any tribal representation, said Noelle Chambers, executive director of the Amah Mutsun Land Trust.
Ethnographic studies conducted through CEQA consultations allowed the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band to protect burial grounds, artifacts and other sacred sites by stopping a proposed sand and gravel mine (https://openspacetrust.org/blog/sargent-ranch/) near Gilroy.
Prop 45 creates a “really harmful” legal precedent in the state by excluding non-federally recognized tribes from the process, Chambers said.
Julia Stein, deputy director of the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the University of California, Los Angeles, calls Prop 45 “a blunt force instrument” that is unlikely to build more projects faster by removing public participation.
It will cause a real loss of community engagement, she said, noting that CEQA is the only avenue for environmental justice communities to influence the environmental impacts of projects in their neighborhoods.
“We lived through a big infrastructure build-out in this country without laws like CEQA in the 1950s and ’60s, and we got environmental justice communities right next to freeways as a result,” Stein said.
CEQA has helped many communities (https://www.phi.org/thought-leadership/act-on-climate-california-communities-addressing-climate-change-and-health/) with elevated rates of asthma, cancer, heart disease and other ailments linked to industrial pollution limit additional harms in their neighborhoods.
A historically overburdened Latino community in southeast Los Angeles used a court order to compel a local government (https://legal-planet.org/2022/02/23/why-ceqa-is-a-useful-tool-for-environmental-justice-communities-in-california/) to review the risks of building an elementary school on a site contaminated with arsenic, and likely lead and asbestos, and require a cleanup. The mostly Latino residents of Riverside County’s Moreno Valley won an agreement to mitigate the harms (https://biologicaldiversity.org/programs/energy-justice/pdfs/WorldLogisticsCenter-Settlement-Agreement-20210429.pdf) on local air quality, climate and wildlife created by heavy-duty trucks serving a 40-million-square-foot warehouse.
Such mitigating measures might never have been identified, let alone required, if Prop 45 had been in effect, opponents say.
In addition to reducing the timeline for public agencies to review projects and fundamentally changing who can provide input, Prop 45 says only the developer or corporation can propose alternatives, said Mabel Tsang, political director for the California Environmental Justice Alliance, which opposes Prop 45.
“That takes away the strongest tool that communities like ours can use to protect ourselves from the worst health impacts before another polluting project is approved next door to our homes,” Tsang said.
Reagan, who signed CEQA as California governor but was known for accelerating deregulation as president, saw environmental protection as a nonpartisan issue. “Preservation of our environment is not a liberal or conservative challenge, it’s common sense,” he said during his 1984 State of the Union (https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/archives/speech/address-joint-session-congress-state-union-january-1984) address.
Now, on the heels of the Trump administration’s attempts to roll back the nation’s major environmental laws, experts say CEQA is more important than ever to safeguard public health and the environment from polluting industries.
Recent polling suggests that on Nov. 3, voters may not approve a measure designed to kneecap California’s most important air- and water-quality protection law.
A poll released Tuesday (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California shows that 50 percent of voters oppose Prop 45, while those who support it dropped to 46 percent from 73 percent in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), when voters knew only general information about the proposition.

Political leaders on both sides of California’s political spectrum have for years argued the “landmark” California Environmental Quality Act has become a well-intentioned mess that delays and halts necessary projects.
Each year, lawmakers carve out narrow CEQA exemptions to jumpstart housing and other projects, but the law remains the main impediment to construction.
Serious reformers call for a far-reaching reform rather than a piecemeal approach where the new exemptions always come with strings attached.
California voters will finally have a chance to approve a broad revamping of CEQA if they approve Proposition 45, which was developed by the California Chamber of Commerce.
Despite claims by opponents, Prop.
45 does not gut a law that requires local agencies to assess the environmental impacts of major projects.
Instead, it tweaks the law in sensible and fair-minded ways that provide quicker approval timelines, reduce meritless lawsuits and limit open-ended demands by local agencies.
CEQA applies to any project that requires a discretionary approval.
The agency often requires developers to provide an Environmental Impact Report (EIR).

### Background
As part of this process, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires an agency to consider how a project might negatively affect the environment before approving it.
CEQA applies to many types of public and private projects, such as housing developments, school facilities, and highway expansions.

Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.”

The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court’s review process for CEQA lawsuits.

#### Protect our environment; vote no on Prop. 45
Re: “Prop.
45 would reform CEQA, speeding the approval process and spurring construction” (Page A14, Oct. 18).
Thumbs down for the Mercury News and East Bay Times’ regrettable yes position on Proposition 45.
...
Proposition 45 would largely dismantle the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), California’s bedrock environmental protection law.
Since 1970, CEQA has ensured that projects that threaten California’s clean air, clean water, tribal assets or invaluable environmental resources receive full public and judicial review before they are built.
While the Chamber of Commerce and Proposition 45’s corporate proponents ramble on about enabling more housing (while most housing is already exempt from CEQA), their true objective is to fast-track polluting projects — including data centers — with far less public and environmental oversight.
Where is the planning that allows human society and nature to succeed together?
Voting no on Proposition 45 provides an opportunity to push back on the rush to development at all costs.
Please join Climate Action California’s thousands of supporters in voting no on Proposition 45.

The California Environmental Quality Act has been used in such an abusive way for more than 50 years that then-Gov. Jerry Brown’s 2012 description of CEQA reform as “the Lord’s work” has gone from being seen as a good one-liner from an unusually witty politician to a profound observation about life in the Golden State.
There is a reason the Legislature has had to pass so many CEQA exemptions:
Many major, valuable projects would never have been built without this protection. The 1970 state law makes it too easy for third parties to block or stall proposals that they don’t like or want to be paid to support. This led directly to a 2017 analysis that documents CEQA’s central role in the state’s decades-old shortage of housing, massively driving up the cost of all types of shelter and impoverishing millions of residents.

Yes, of course, some CEQA lawsuits are defensible and necessary.
But when you see the range of organizations that have vowed support for Proposition 45 — a modest CEQA reform on the November ballot sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce — it’s eye-opening.
The California Hospital Association, the California Farm Bureau, the California Senior Alliance and more than a half-dozen clean energy groups are among a vast list of institutions seeking relief from the migraines they face because of the broadly written, vague law.
Prop. 45 would impose a 365-day limit on official environmental reviews for projects ranging from broadband construction to building roads, homes and schools to wildfire mitigation. Courts would be given a maximum of 270 days to rule on CEQA suits after they are filed.
Contrary to claims that the changes would gut “the state’s strongest-in-the-nation environmental laws,” local governments would still have considerable authority in the approval process. Activists wouldn’t be muzzled.
This is reflected in the analysis of Prop. 45 from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
The LAO’s biggest concern had to do with potentially substantial implementation costs for state and local governments, not weakened green regulations. And the analysis also noted the benefit to governments of new revenue from ventures no longer blocked by CEQA — and from having their own projects cost less.
Prop. 45 won’t transform the state’s regulatory maze overnight. But it would make California’s planning approval process fairer, less expensive and considerably more predictable.
Yes on 45.

The debate over Prop. 45 is about California’s building future. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 3:21 PM
Cows pasture on land near Scott Road and Carson Creek in Sacramento County on Wednesday, Nov. 27, 2024. Proposition 45 seeks to streamline CEQA for California projects like housing, water and clean energy, raising concerns about reduced review and potential environmental harm.
Hector Amezcua
hamezcua@sacbee.com
If approved by voters in November,Proposition 45 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317117913.html) would significantly change how California reviews and approves construction projects, including affordable housing, under the California Environmental Quality Act. CEQA, California’s most important land use law, has too often been weaponized by not-in-my-backyard interests (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article316418885.html) to stop the construction of needed housing. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article316418885.html)
Prop. 45 seeks to bring long-needed reform to CEQA provisions that can add substantial costs to new homes, hospitals, water systems, roads, bridges and clean energy projects.
The initiative targets frivolous lawsuits and bureaucratic red tape that makes construction too slow and too costly. It proposes to streamline the permitting process without weakening the state’s environmental laws.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 45 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317117913.html)
Projects often make it through CEQA only to be stopped at the back end by litigation. Currently, a project can go through lengthy environmental reviews, be approved by a local government and still be sued under CEQA. In such cases, courts often order additional review, which adds to the cost of a project or, in some cases, spell the project’s end.
McClatchy’s California editorial board, representing The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/) Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) andSan Luis Obispo Tribune, (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommends a “Yes” vote on Prop. 45.
“This isn’t about us running away from protecting the environment,” Dan Dunmoyer, president and CEO of the California Building Industry Association, told us. “This is about bringing what I call ‘the sweet spot,’ the balance, to protecting our environment.” Dunmoyer is right. Building more housing in California creates more opportunities for more people to stay and build lives with their families.
Prop. 45 would also limit parts of the CEQA process, including the often interminable length of public-comment periods for projects. It would limit judges from halting entire projects when they find a CEQA violation. Instead, judges would only be empowered to halt the portion of projects found in violation CEQA until corrections are made.
The initiative would also change the state’s tribal consultation requirements, limiting the mandatory consultation to only federally recognized tribes for projects using the new procedures, strengthening government-to-government consultation by ensuring early tribal engagement and enhancing confidentiality protections.
“Every year a project is delayed again means higher financing costs, construction inflation, legal expenses … and those costs don’t disappear,” said campaign consultant, Emma Manoukian Chung. “Prop. 45 (builds) more of what Californians need, and we stop wasting money on unnecessary delay.”
Those in support of Prop. 45 include the California Building Industry Association, California Business Roundtable, California Chamber of Commerce and California Council for Affordable Housing. (https://californiacouncil.org/) Those in opposition include the California Democratic Party, the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California (https://cabuildingtrades.org/) and Sierra Club of California.
By imposing stricter deadlines on government agencies to complete environmental reviews, Proposition 45 would allow housing, transportation, water and health care projects to move forward more quickly and at lower cost without weakening California’s environmental protections.
That’s the goal behind Prop. 45 — and it’s long overdue.

Proposition 45: No Recommendation
September 23, 2026
Share
Share this page on Twitter (https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-45-2026%2F&text=Proposition+45%3A+%3Cspan+class%3D%22dewidow%22%3ENo+Recommendation%3C%2Fspan%3E)
Share this page on Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-45-2026%2F&t=Proposition%2045:%20No%20Recommendation)
Share this page via Email (mailto:?subject=Proposition+45%3A+%3Cspan+class%3D%22dewidow%22%3ENo+Recommendation%3C%2Fspan%3E+-+California+YIMBY&body=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-45-2026%2F)
by Max Dubler
Introduction
While Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) meaningfully touches on housing, it will have a much more significant impact on non-housing projects. Pro-housing voters should consider the arguments for and against the measure and make their own decision based on their values.
Analysis
Background: The California Environmental Quality Act
Passed in 1970 and signed into law by then-Governor Reagan, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA, say “SEE-kwah”) required government agencies to study and publicize the potential environmental impacts of public projects like dams, highways, and power plants, and gave the public the right to sue if they do not believe the impact analysis is sufficient. The scope of the law was massively expanded when the courts ruled that any project that requires public approval is a “public project.” This empowered a wide variety of interests to use the CEQA process to delay or block projects they don’t like.
Last year, the state legislature passed AB 130 (https://cayimby.org/legislation/ab-609/), which exempted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) “infill” housing, broadly defined [1] as homes in existing developed areas, from environmental review under CEQA. This was a major victory for California YIMBY, which has long sought this exemption and sponsored AB 609, which was incorporated into AB 130.
What does Prop 45 do?
Creates an alternative, opt-in process with strict “shot clocks” for environmental review (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-local-timelines) for “essential” housing, water, transportation ( excluding high speed rail), clean energy, transmission, broadband, and healthcare infrastructure. Environmental review for these projects must be completed within 365 business days, or about a year and a half. There are shorter timelines for determining application completeness (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-completeness) (30 days) and lesser levels of environmental review (180 days for a negative declaration or a mitigated negative declaration).
Creates a 90-day shot clock for “any and all” public agency approvals required for essential projects besides CEQA, including building permits, Coastal Development Permits, and utility approvals.
Requires tribal consultation for all projects, AB 130 labor standards for housing projects (except 100% affordable projects under 85’), and Section 21183.5 labor standards (https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prc/division-13/chapter-6-5/section-21183-5/) for other projects that use this environmental review pathway.
Limits public comment on environmental reviews to 45 days (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-public-comment).
Limits the scope of “alternative projects” that must be analyzed (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-alternatives) in the environmental review process to one alternative proposed by the applicant and a “no project” alternative.
Creates a new evidentiary standard for environmental impacts (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-impacts) requiring that they only be found significant if they violate objective, quantifiable standards already in existing law (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-judicial-scope) when a project is proposed, and freezes those standards on the date a project application is filed (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-impacts). This would eliminate public agencies’ broad discretion to explore project alternatives and negotiate environmental mitigations.
Curtails (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-remedies) courts’ ability to block projects in their entirety. If a legal challenge to a project’s environmental review is successful, the remedy is limited to the specific issue identified in the lawsuit. The courts can’t order an agency to rescind its approval of the broader project.
Broadly, Prop 45 tightens up the environmental review process. It will make it easier to build infrastructure and other large scale projects by curtailing potential litigants’ ability to slow down and block construction by filing lawsuits challenging projects’ environmental impact analyses.
How does this affect housing?
Prop 45 would affect housing in two major ways: first, it would make it easier to build housing projects [2], mostly new subdivisions, that do not qualify for the AB 130 infill exemption, as well as the infrastructure necessary to service those housing projects. Second, it would significantly speed public agency approvals for housing projects that use this environmental review process.
The labor provisions in AB 130, the existing CEQA infill exemption, would apply (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-housing-labor) to projects that use the Prop 45 environmental review process unless (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-mandatory-parts) they are also using a different streamlining law that mandates prevailing wages or a project labor requirement, in which case they would have to abide by those requirements.
While Prop 45 will speed public agency approvals for all housing, it will also make it easier to build car-dependent sprawl housing and the freeways and water infrastructure necessary to serve that sprawl.
What does California YIMBY think of this?
While this measure does affect housing, it’s not primarily about housing. Rather, it’s about reining in an out of control CEQA process (https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2021/03/signature-environmental-law-hurts-housing/618264/) that has ballooned far beyond what the legislature intended in 1970 and made building large projects slow and expensive (https://www.mercurynews.com/2025/04/20/ceqa-california-high-speed-rail/?share=aft0p2r22rr2itegarfi).
Prop 45 would reform CEQA by bringing policy ideas that have worked to streamline housing permitting—shot clocks, objective standards that vest at the time of an application, limited agency discretion to expand the scope of review, narrow remedies, etc—to the environmental review process.
Whether this is a good idea depends on how you weigh the tradeoffs: is permitting new wind and solar energy infrastructure faster worth making it easier to build freeways? Should we make it easier to build transmission lines to carry that clean energy to consumers, even if it means potentially impacting wildlife habitat? Zooming out, is litigation about the public disclosure of environmental impacts (https://history.yale.edu/publications/public-citizens-attack-big-government-and-remaking-american-liberalism) really the best way to weigh the environmental costs of large projects against their potential public benefits and ensure that communities have a voice in what’s built near them?
These are big fundamental questions about growth, sustainability, and the proper structure of democratic decision-making.
Narrowing the focus to housing, the central question here is how you feel about sprawl. California YIMBY works to make it easier to build new homes in our existing cities and towns, where we already have infrastructure to serve them. As we have said before (https://cayimby.org/news-events/statement-in-support-of-the-east-solano-plan/):
“When it comes to solving our housing crisis, our focus remains on making it easier to build housing in existing cities—near quality jobs and public services. Toward this end, we have worked to liberalize (https://cayimby.org/reports/california-adu-reform-a-retrospective/) zoning, streamline (https://cayimby.org/legislation/sb-330/) permitting, and reduce (https://cayimby.org/legislation/ab-2097/) costs. We believe we can (and must) solve the housing and climate crises simultaneously. That means building communities with denser housing and alternatives to automobile dependence.”
That said, we support building well-designed new cities (https://cayimby.org/news-events/statement-in-support-of-the-east-solano-plan/) and we realize that some greenfield development will necessarily be part of solving our housing shortage. Given the scale of the housing crisis, we need all the new housing we can get. Further, lots of people want single family homes on larger lots; and they should be able to have them, to the extent that is sustainable and feasible.
Still, our friends in the environmental movement have raised significant substantive concerns (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-baca-initiative/) about this measure. Most relevant to housing voters: we should not be building new homes in the fire-prone wildland urban interface (https://cayimby.org/blog/the-impact-of-land-use-planning-on-wildfire-risk-a-study-in-southern-california/) because doing so puts people in harm’s way (https://cayimby.org/blog/how-the-northwests-wildfire-crisis-is-a-sprawl-crisis/) and exacerbates our insurance crisis (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-07-22/californians-are-subsidizing-mansion-wildfire-insurance-as-fair-risk-explodes). The fact that Prop 45 makes it easier to build freeways but not high speed rail also gives us pause.
The bottom line: there are good reasons to support this measure and good reasons to oppose it. Housing voters should consider it in light of broader concerns about climate and sustainability.
Recommendation: Neutral
Further Reading
Ballotpedia analysis (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_45,_Changes_to_Environmental_Review_Process_for_Certain_Projects_Initiative_(2026)), “yes” endorsement from Circulate Planning and Policy (https://www.circulatesd.org/why_circulate_supports_prop_45), “no” endorsement from Greenbelt Alliance (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-baca-initiative/), annotated measure text from GrowSF (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/), Legislative Analyst’s Office analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026), Public Citizens: The Attack on Big Government and the Remaking of American Liberalism (https://history.yale.edu/publications/public-citizens-attack-big-government-and-remaking-american-liberalism) (book)
Notes
[1] AB 130 defines an “infill” project as one where the project site meets any of the following criteria:
(A) Has been previously developed with an urban use.
(B) At least 75 percent of the perimeter of the site adjoins parcels that are developed with urban uses.
(C) At least 75 percent of the area within a one-quarter mile radius of the site is developed with urban uses.
(D) For sites with four sides, at least three out of four sides are developed with urban uses and at least two-thirds of the perimeter of the site adjoins parcels that are developed with urban uses.
”Urban use” means any current or previous residential or commercial development, public institution, or public park that is surrounded by other urban uses, parking lot or structure, transit or transportation passenger facility, or retail use, or any combination of those uses.
[2] The measure’s definition of “essential housing projects” is extremely broad, encompassing residential projects; mixed-use projects; transitional housing, emergency shelters, and supportive housing; farmworker housing; group living accommodations like monasteries; student housing of all types; senior housing; new subdivisions; and adaptive reuse of commercial buildings.

Two Takes: Should California pass Prop 45 to limit CEQA reviews for ‘essential’ projects?
By Alex Jackson , Benjamin Lu , Contributors Oct 11, 2026
A BART train departs the station near the site of a new construction project that will bring modular housing to the El Cerrito BART station, in El Cerrito, Calif., on Wednesday, March 4, 2026. Related California is starting the 780 unit development meant to provide affordable housing and increase transit ridership.,
Carlos Avila Gonzalez/S.F. Chronicle
Enacted in 1970, the California Environmental Quality Act (https://oag.ca.gov/environment/ceqa) requires state and local agencies to “evaluate the significant environmental impacts of proposed projects” and allows citizens to sue if they feel that the agencies have failed to do so.
Such lawsuits have often resulted in years-long delays for new housing developments, and the act, known as CEQA, is often cited as a central factor in California’s affordability crisis. Lawmakers of both political parties have scrambled to find workarounds to jump-start construction projects. Senate Bill 79, which took effect this year, established a carve-out that exempts new housing construction along transit corridors from CEQA review.

Proposition 45, a November ballot measure, is another attempt to scale back CEQA. It proposes streamlining roadblocks on projects deemed “essential,” including the construction of roads, bridges, housing and schools. The measure would also limit environmental review to 365 days and require courts to rule on CEQA challenges within 270 days of a lawsuit being filed.
We asked two experts with opposing views — Alex Jackson and Benjamin Lu — to offer their perspectives on Prop 45. After reading both perspectives, please leave a comment.
Measure will help state meet clean energy goals
California has set ambitious clean energy targets, including 100% clean electricity and economy-wide carbon neutrality by 2045. Meeting those goals entails more renewable generation, battery storage, transmission and grid infrastructure — and building it fast.
The shift away from fossil fuels must also be done affordably, so the cost of the clean energy transition doesn’t fall on consumers. Unfortunately, too many clean energy projects spend years navigating environmental review, permitting and litigation, raising costs and slowing essential progress.
That’s why I support Proposition 45, to help California build clean energy and other essential infrastructure faster and more affordably. Prop 45 puts clear, enforceable timelines around the permitting and review process so the clean energy projects California is counting on get built on schedule and on budget.
I spent 12 years as a senior attorney at the Natural Resources Defense Council helping advance some of California’s signature climate policies. Today, I lead American Clean Power-California, representing wind, solar, storage and transmission companies. From both perspectives, one thing is clear: Setting ambitious clean energy goals is the easy part. Building the infrastructure to meet them is the challenge.
California isn’t simply swapping out old power plants for new ones — we’re asking the grid to power more vehicles, more buildings and more businesses at once. We can’t retire fossil fuel plants until clean replacements are online, and the state’s energy agencies project that we must add roughly 8,000 megawatts of new clean energy and storage resources to the grid every year for the next two decades.
Consider the Panoche Valley solar project in San Benito County. Approved by the county in 2010 at roughly 420 megawatts, the project faced a lawsuit over its environmental review. Opponents lost, appealed and lost again, then brought a third challenge after the developer revised the project. By the time it finally began operating eight years later, it had been cut to less than a third of its original size.
Prop 45 would have addressed the Panoche Valley project's challenges at every stage. Prop 45 sets deadlines from application completeness and environmental review through remaining agency approvals and litigation. Prop 45 does this while maintaining California’s bedrock environmental laws and protections and retaining local control and community input. Local governments keep their authority to approve or deny projects in their own communities, and citizens keep a meaningful voice throughout the process.
We don’t have to choose between environmental protection and building the clean energy infrastructure it needs to address climate change. Building that infrastructure is environmental protection at scale, and Prop 45 shows how to do it right: preserving environmental standards while curbing frivolous lawsuits and delays so legitimate concerns get resolved and clean energy projects get built.

Rolling back oversight puts air quality at risk
Proposition 45 asks voters a simple question: Will you trade critical public health and environmental protections so industry can build polluting projects a little faster?
This measure significantly limits public oversight over a wide range of such projects, from freeway expansions to heavy industrial uses like biomass plants. Some legal experts also believe Prop 45 could be used to fast-track data centers in many cases.
Meanwhile, federal clean air protections are being aggressively rolled back, especially in California. The American Lung Association’s “State of the Air” 2026 report (https://www.lung.org/research/sota)identifies the cities most heavily burdened by air pollution nationwide. Of the 24 U.S. metropolitan areas with the highest levels of smog, eight are in California, including the San Jose-San Francisco-Oakland region.

Heavy truck traffic on freeways and industrial activity generate particulate pollution, which is closely associated with asthma, cardiovascular disease, lung cancer, premature death, low birth weights and outdoor worker illnesses. By limiting safeguards against pollution, Prop 45 increases the risk of lung-related illnesses.
The California Environmental Quality Act requires potentially polluting projects to limit health impacts to the extent feasible. This process can take time. On balance, the current approach to weight development and public health is working. California has the fourth-largest gross domestic product in the world, and its economy is growing at a faster pace than that of states like Texas and Florida. These facts make it hard to justify sacrificing health protections to speed up development.
California needs more housing — but Prop 45 promises more sprawl. Last year, the state exempted nearly all urban housing from environmental review. Prop 45 instead speeds up development in areas with high wildfire risk and longer commutes. More sprawl inevitably leads to wider freeways and dirtier air.
For families living near existing pollution sources, public oversight is often the only way to protect themselves from the health impacts associated with new industrial development.
Air pollution drives up medical expenses for families and the state’s healthcare system. Higher incidence of childhood asthma increases visits to cash-strapped emergency rooms. The cognitive effects of lung pollution even make it harder for children to succeed in school.

Data center developers, PG&E and other special interests have contributed tens of millions of dollars to pass Prop 45. Voters should know that nothing in the initiative requires direct savings for everyday Californians.
The trade-offs Prop 45 promises aren’t worth the risks. California is healthier and stronger without it.
Dr. Benjamin Lu is the advocacy manager for clean air policy at the American Lung Association for California.
